# Legal requirements
Distilled from: the company's legal memo on comparative content and content marketing.

## Applicability
- Strict for OWNED articles (the Example Co blog, in the company's voice). Soft for THIRD-PARTY articles published under an outside author (apply where reasonable, not strictly).
- Source of truth for voice/legal already enforced by the copywriter skill = the skill. This card covers only the gaps / the legal specifics not in the skill.

## Rules (verbatim-critical)
- Comparative content (rankings / "top / best" pages, "X vs Y", "alternatives to <competitor>") is permitted in all covered jurisdictions ONLY if truthful, objective, and non-misleading. The same legal regime applies whether published as a "ranking" or a "comparison".
- Every comparative or superlative claim MUST be substantiated with evidence (sources, tests, studies, documents) available before publication. No claim ships without its proof.
- NO unsubstantiated superlatives: never "best", "fastest", "cheapest", "most reliable", "#1", "first" etc. without cited backing. Replace with qualified, sourced forms — e.g. "one of the best by <metric>", "according to study X, faster", "X% of clients report... (source)", "fees reduced by Y% vs peers [source]".
- NO incorrect/vague comparisons: comparisons without concrete, verifiable characteristics, or based on false data, are prohibited (EU Directive 2006/114/EC; German UWG §6; UK CAP Code 3.32–3.36; US Lanham Act §43(a)).
- NO disparagement / denigration / defamation of competitors. Cannot call a competitor "least reliable", "overpriced", "worse quality" etc. without proof. Negative information must be substantiated and true. Direct or even indirect slander/insult is prohibited.
- Comparisons must be of products/services of similar purpose, on objective, relevant, verifiable attributes (including price, where public).
- Competitor names and logos MAY be used only nominatively / for identification ("nominative fair use"), only where genuinely necessary and justified, and only when the underlying claim is verified. Do NOT: create confusion or false impression of sponsorship/endorsement; restyle a competitor's logo to resemble Example Co's brand; unfairly exploit the competitor's reputation.
- Competitor logos: add alt-text identifying it ("<Company X> logo"); where appropriate cite source and mark "TM" for registered trademarks.
- Implicit identification counts: even without naming a competitor, if context clearly points to one, the same comparison/defamation rules apply and can ground a claim.
- Sponsorship / paid-relationship disclosure is MANDATORY for any material funded or authored by Example Co that could read as independent. Hidden advertising (paid content presented as a neutral/independent review) is itself unlawful (EU, US FTC, UK CMA/ASA). Disclose the material connection:
  - US / UK: label "Advert", "Advertisement Feature" (advertorial); "#ad" on social.
  - DE: "Anzeige" or "Werbung"; in other EU markets the local equivalent of "sponsored material" / "prepared with the support of company X".
  - Add a disclaimer stating it is a sponsored material, not an independent review (at the start or end).
- Authorship must be clear; do NOT publish content paid for by Example Co as a genuinely "independent expert" review without the disclosure above.
- Cross-border default: when content is reachable in multiple countries, comply with the local law of each target market; when in doubt, apply the STRICTEST standard (EU + UK + FTC) as a global safe harbor.

## Notes / context
- Scope of the source: B2B software for work with independent contractors, compared against other vendors in the same market (Northwind, Contoso, Fabrikam, etc.) via SEO rankings and comparison pages. Maps directly to Example Co competitor-comparison and "top/best" articles.
- Five core risk categories: (1) false/misleading advertising, (2) competitor trademark infringement, (3) unfair competition, (4) defamation / reputational harm, (5) hidden advertising / mislabeling.
- Jurisdiction notes: EU — Directive 2006/114/EC (nominative use of a competitor's mark in a lawful comparison is permitted); Germany — UWG §6 on comparative advertising; US — FTC policy ("Truthful and nondeceptive comparative claims are allowed") + Lanham Act §43(a) + FTC material-connection disclosure; UK — CAP Code (rules 2.1/2.4 transparency, 3.32–3.36 comparisons), enforced by ASA, substantiation required; Canada/Australia/Singapore — same principles (Australia ACCC requires sponsorship disclosure); some markets (Japan, China) are culturally sensitive about naming competitors.
- Jurisdiction can be steered in practice via geo-targeting, content language, local authors/platforms, distribution targeting, localized adaptations (wording, disclaimers, criteria), and geo-gating sensitive content.
- Pre-publish checklist (from source): all comparative claims provable; no impermissible/misleading wording; competitor logos handled correctly; authorship/sponsorship marked; legal/compliance review against the applicable jurisdiction's ad rules.
- Approved phrasing pattern: "According to independent testing, an invoice passes approval in half as many steps as in [competitor] [source]"; "The price is in some cases lower than competitors' (see comparison below)". Banned: "fastest on the market" / "competitors are overpriced and lower quality" (no proof).
- Overlap with the copywriter skill (do NOT duplicate): the skill already bans unsubstantiated superlatives and subjective claims without data (BLOCK 2) and vague marketing words — this card extends that to the legal substantiation, competitor-trademark, and sponsorship-disclosure obligations the skill does not cover. The skill's positioning rules (category labels, speed and guarantee wording next to the product) are separate brand concerns, not in scope here.
